explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Pharaoh, Egypt's king, was angry with his chief cupbearer and chief baker, and he put them in the captain of the guard's house, “the same prison where Joseph was confined.” (Genesis 40:3) Joseph didn't have to go looking for company. Two of the king's own officers got delivered right to him.

Not this time, friend. Verse 3 says Pharaoh imprisoned them in the house of the captain of the guard, “the same prison where Joseph was confined.” So there was no separate cell for the king's officers. Pharaoh, Egypt's king, put them right where Joseph already was.

Joseph it is. The captain of the guard assigned the two officers to him, and verse 4 says he became their personal attendant. So a man held in that prison is now looking after two of Pharaoh's officers. I think that's a strange spot to be in, and he does it anyway.

Reuben was one of Jacob's sons, so he was Joseph's brother (Genesis 35:23). But he isn't in this prison scene at all. The text says the captain of the guard assigned the cupbearer and the baker to Joseph, who became their personal attendant. Joseph is the one standing in that doorway.

Benjamin was another of Jacob's sons and a brother to Joseph (Genesis 35:24). Good name to know, friend, but he isn't in this scene. Verse 4 says the captain of the guard assigned the two officers to Joseph, and Joseph became their personal attendant. That's the man on the job.

Distraught is the word, friend. Verse 6 says that's what Joseph saw when he came to them in the morning. That's more than a rough night's sleep. Whatever those dreams were, they left these two in a heavy place.

Relieved would make a nice morning, but that's not what Joseph saw. The text says the two men were distraught. Each of them had a dream that night and neither one had peace on his face. I bet Joseph noticed it the second he walked in.

Nobody in that prison house was whistling, friend. Verse 6 says Joseph saw that the two men were distraught. Cheerful faces don't get a question about them, but these faces did. So Joseph asks about them in the very next verse.

That's the trouble, friend. They tell Joseph, “We both had dreams,” and then, “…but there is no one to interpret them.” (Genesis 40:8) They have the dreams in hand already. What they don't have is anyone to tell them what the dreams mean.

The text doesn't say that. They tell Joseph they both had dreams, “…but there is no one to interpret them.” (Genesis 40:8) Joseph asks them to tell him their dreams, and each man does. The details are fine. It's the meaning they're missing.

That's not in the text, friend. Verse 5 says both men had a dream on the same night, and in verse 8 they say, “…but there is no one to interpret them.” Nothing there says the dreams repeat. The trouble is that nobody could tell them what the dreams meant.

God is the answer. Joseph asks, “Don’t interpretations belong to God?” and then tells the men, “Tell me your dreams.” (Genesis 40:8) Notice where he points. He doesn't put himself at the center of the room, friend. He points up.

Pharaoh was the king who locked these two up, so I see why he came to mind. But Joseph doesn't say interpretations belong to him. In verse 8 he asks, “Don’t interpretations belong to God?” His answer goes way above any throne in Egypt.

Nobody in this scene brings up magicians, friend. When the two men say no one can interpret their dreams, Joseph asks, “Don’t interpretations belong to God?” (Genesis 40:8) That's where he sends them. Then he invites them to tell him the dreams.

explanations.answer: Squeezes the grapes into it for Pharaoh
explanations.explanation: That's the dream. The cupbearer says, “…I took the grapes, squeezed them into his cup, and placed the cup in his hand.” (Genesis 40:11) Fresh-squeezed service, straight to the king. The cupbearer was doing the job he knew.

explanations.answer: Pours the cup out on the ground
explanations.explanation: Nothing gets poured out in that dream, friend. The cupbearer says he took the grapes, squeezed them into the cup, “…and placed the cup in his hand.” (Genesis 40:11) The cup goes into Pharaoh's hand. That detail matters when Joseph explains it.

That would be a very different dream, friend. The cupbearer says he squeezed the grapes into Pharaoh's cup, “…and placed the cup in his hand.” (Genesis 40:11) The cup goes to Pharaoh, not to the cupbearer's own lips. He was serving the king.

That's what Joseph says. “Within three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore your position.” (Genesis 40:13) Then he adds that the cupbearer will put Pharaoh's cup in his hand, just as he did before. Good news, and it comes with a clock of three days.

explanations.answer: Give him a seat on his council
explanations.explanation: A council seat isn't in the text, friend. Joseph says Pharaoh will lift up the cupbearer's head and restore his position. Then he says, “You will put Pharaoh’s cup in his hand, just as you did when you were his cupbearer.” (Genesis 40:13) It's the old job, back again.

explanations.answer: Put him in charge of the prison
explanations.explanation: That's not what Joseph says. The prison is where the cupbearer is stuck, so I see why it came to mind. But Joseph says Pharaoh will restore his position, and that he will put Pharaoh's cup in his hand “…just as you did when you were his cupbearer.” (Genesis 40:13) That's a ticket out of the prison, not a job in it.

It's the other way around, friend. Joseph says, “…even here I have done nothing for which they should have put me in this dungeon.” (Genesis 40:15) He also says he was kidnapped from the land of the Hebrews. He is saying he doesn't belong in that dungeon.

False is right, friend. Joseph tells the cupbearer, “…even here I have done nothing for which they should have put me in this dungeon.” (Genesis 40:15) He says it right after telling how he was kidnapped. He is asking to be remembered, and he is saying plainly that he doesn't belong there.

Three is right. The chief baker says, “…three baskets of white bread on my head.” (Genesis 40:16) Three is also the number in the cupbearer's dream, where there were three branches. Joseph is about to tell the baker what those baskets mean.

Seven is a big number in the Bible, but not here, friend. The baker says, “…three baskets of white bread on my head.” (Genesis 40:16) Three baskets, stacked up on one head. That's the number Joseph works with.

Close to it, but one basket short. The baker says, “…three baskets of white bread on my head.” (Genesis 40:16) That's a tall stack to carry around. And the number three matters when Joseph explains the dream.

explanations.answer: Birds are eating them out of the basket
explanations.explanation: That's what the baker sees. In the top basket are all sorts of baked goods for Pharaoh, “…but the birds were eating them out of the basket on my head.” (Genesis 40:17) Me, I'd be waving my mustache at those birds and hollering. In the dream, the baked goods meant for Pharaoh never reach him.

explanations.answer: They are tumbling down to the ground
explanations.explanation: Nothing tumbles in that dream, friend. The baker says the birds “…were eating them out of the basket on my head.” (Genesis 40:17) The basket stays put on his head. The birds are the ones making the trouble.

explanations.answer: Servants are carrying them all away
explanations.explanation: No servants show up in the baker's dream. He says the top basket held all sorts of baked goods for Pharaoh, “…but the birds were eating them out of the basket on my head.” (Genesis 40:17) The birds are the ones doing the taking. The baked goods never get to Pharaoh.

The two interpretations don't match, friend. The cupbearer got good news, and the baker didn't. Joseph tells the baker, “Within three days Pharaoh will lift off your head and hang you on a tree.” (Genesis 40:19) I think this is a hard part of the story, and it deserves to be taken seriously.

False is right, friend, and it's a heavy one. Joseph tells the baker, “Within three days Pharaoh will lift off your head and hang you on a tree.” (Genesis 40:19) The cupbearer's dream pointed to being restored, and the baker's pointed the other way. I think this part of the story hurts.

It's Pharaoh's birthday. Verse 20 says, “On the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, he held a feast for all his officials.” That's the same three days Joseph gave both men. A feast for all those officials is a whole lot of cookie boxes, if you ask me.

No battle is mentioned in this passage, friend. Verse 20 says the third day was Pharaoh's birthday, and he held a feast for all his officials. It was the third day, just as Joseph had said. Nobody in the story brings up a war.

The harvest doesn't come up in this passage. Verse 20 says, “On the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, he held a feast for all his officials.” So the feast was for Pharaoh's birthday. That's the day the three days run out.

True, and it's a sober one. Verse 22 says, “But Pharaoh hanged the chief baker, just as Joseph had described to them in his interpretation.” The three days passed and what Joseph said came to pass. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the story.

It does match, friend, and it's a heavy moment. Verse 22 says Pharaoh hanged the chief baker, “…just as Joseph had described to them in his interpretation.” What Joseph said happened. I think this one hurts to read.

That's what the text says. “The chief cupbearer, however, did not remember Joseph; he forgot all about him.” (Genesis 40:23) Joseph had asked him to mention him to Pharaoh so he could be brought out of the prison. I think that stings, since the cupbearer had just walked out of the same prison.

That's what Joseph asked for, friend, but it's not what happened. Verse 23 says the cupbearer “…did not remember Joseph; he forgot all about him.” Joseph is still in the prison when this passage ends. The ask was never carried out.

explanations.answer: He sends for Joseph right away
explanations.explanation: That would have been a quick turnaround, but that's not the text. Verse 23 says the cupbearer “…did not remember Joseph; he forgot all about him.” Joseph had asked to be remembered and mentioned to Pharaoh. He's still waiting.
